newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's ex-partner sentenced to 3 years in prison.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's ex-partner sentenced to 3 years in prison.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's former Whitewater business partner James McDougal was sentenced to three years in prison Monday after making a deal that could spell trouble for the White House.

McDougal, 56, had faced up to 81 years in prison for his conviction last May on 18 counts of fraud and conspiracy, but got off lightly because of his full cooperation with Whitewater independent prosecutor Kenneth Starr.

McDougal hinted to reporters afterwards that he had given investigators information that could implicate the president and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton in the Whitewater scandal and urged everyone to "stay tuned" to developments.
When asked if he believed the Clintons would be exonerated in the scandal, as he had maintained throught his trial, McDougal said simply: "I wouldn't go to the bank on that."
Apart from the three years in prison, U.S. District Judge George Howard gave McDougal a three-year probated sentence, with the first year to be served under house arrest, and a $10,000 fine.
He recommended that McDougal serve his time in a prison hospital because of a variety of severe health problems and ordered him to report to prison on June 16.

McDougal said he would likely appeal the case but was apologetic in court, telling Howard he took "full and complete responsibility for my crimes and misdeeds" and that he had "no excuse whatsoever to offer your honour."

Starr argued for a light sentence for McDougal, whom he said had provided investigators "information on a wide range of matters," including items that were previously known only to a "very small group of people."
He said McDougal had led his team to new documentary evidence and witnesses that "independently corroborate substantial portions of Mr. McDougal's account" but gave no further details.
McDougal has been the central figure of the Whitewater saga since it flared up in 1993 and was far closer to Clinton than anyone else brought to trial in the investigation.
He came under federal investigation when his Madison Guaranty Savings and Loan was declared insolvent and shut in 1989 at a cost of about $65 million to taxpayers.
At his trial, he was found guilty of using up to $3 million in fraudulent federally backed loans to help finance several Arkansas real estate projects in the mid-1980s.
McDougal had ridiculed Starr and his team of attorneys as "Republican henchmen" and said he would never cooperate with them, but quickly changed his tune after his convictions.

Since then, he has reportedly corroborated allegations by Arkansas banker David Hale that Clinton, then Arkansas governor, pressured Hale into extending an illegal $300,000 loan to McDougal's former wife Susan in 1986.
Prosecutors alleged that $50,000 from the loan was funnelled into the flagging Whitewater real estate project in which the McDougals and the Clintons were business partners in the 1980s.
Clinton and McDougal flatly denied Hale's allegations and legal experts said Starr's team would need corroborating evidence because McDougal's credibility as a prosecution witness would be weak.
But McDougal said Monday he was able to back up his version of events. "The documentary evidence will substantiate anything I have said to the independent counsel," he said.
Starr's team has also questioned McDougal on another fraudulent real estate venture known as Castle Grande.

Hillary Rodham Clinton performed some legal work for Madison Guaranty as a private attorney and Starr is investigating whether she was aware of illegal financing for the Castle Grande project. She has denied any wrongdoing.

Susan McDougal was convicted with her former husband last year and was sentenced to two years in prison for her role in the fraudulent loan schemes. But she refused to cooperate with Starr and is currently serving a contempt of court sentence because she refused a judge's order to answer questions before a Whitewater grand jury.
She has said James McDougal told her he was lying to win a reduced sentence and that he urged her to do the same.
McDougal denied inventing evidence in order to save himself from a long prison term and hinted that he thought the sentence was fair.

Howard also ordered McDougal to pay $4.72 million in restitution to federal agencies if he ever possesses the financial resources to do so, but that is considered highly unlikely as he has little money, is in poor health and currently lives in a rented mobile home.
